title: Assertions that explain themselves
summary: Pick the assertion whose failure message tells the story: Equal on collections, Equivalent for object graphs, Throws versus ThrowsAny, ThrowsAsync for async code, Single, Collection and Contains.

steps.title: The failure message is the product
body: Both of these fail when the cart has the wrong items. Only one tells you how:
Assert.True(cart.Items.Count == 2);        // Assert.True() Failure. Expected: True. Actual: False
Assert.Equal(["mug", "tea"], cart.Items);   // Assert.Equal() Failure: Collections differ
Reach for the assertion that **knows what you are comparing**:
| two values or two sequences, in order | `Assert.Equal(expected, actual)` |
| two object graphs by their public data (DTOs, records with lists) | `Assert.Equivalent(expected, actual)` |
| exactly one item, and get it | `var line = Assert.Single(order.Lines);` |
| each item in order, with its own checks | `Assert.Collection(items, a => ..., b => ...)` |
| an item is present / a substring | `Assert.Contains(...)`, `Assert.DoesNotContain(...)` |
`Assert.True(condition)` is for real booleans (`IsValid`), not a way to compare values.

steps.prompt: Match each check to the assertion a reviewer would expect.
pairs: the order has exactly one line, then check its SKU
a receipt DTO matches field by field, lists included
the log message mentions the order id
the cart is empty after checkout
three events, each with its own checks, in order

steps.title: Exceptions: Throws, ThrowsAny and ThrowsAsync
body: Throwing is behaviour, so test it. `Assert.Throws<T>` passes only for **exactly** `T` and returns the exception, so you can check its details:

- `Assert.Throws<ArgumentException>` **fails** for `ArgumentNullException` (a subclass). That strictness is deliberate: the API promised one type. Use `Assert.ThrowsAny<ArgumentException>` when any subclass is fine.
- For async code, **await** `Assert.ThrowsAsync<T>`. Without `await`, the test ends before the task does and passes no matter what:
`TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` is cancelled when the run is aborted or the test times out, so pass it to async calls (xUnit's analyzer xUnit1051 asks for it).

steps.prompt: This test passes even though `PlaceAsync` never throws. Why?
options: The returned task is never awaited, so the assertion's result is thrown away when the test returns
The order list must not be empty
steps.explain: `ThrowsAsync` returns a `Task` that fails later. The test method is `void` and does not await it, so it finishes green first. Make the test `async Task` and `await` the assertion. xUnit's analyzer flags this (xUnit2021).

steps.prompt: `Assert.Throws<T>` is strict about the type. What does this plain C# program print? (It mirrors the check xUnit makes.)
steps.explain: `Throws<T>` compares the exact type, `ThrowsAny<T>` accepts subclasses. An `ArgumentNullException` is an `ArgumentException`, but not exactly one.

steps.title: Test an async order desk
prompt: The order desk below is compiled beside your tests:
```csharp
public record OrderLine(string Sku, int Quantity);
public record Receipt(int Id, string Customer, IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines, decimal Total);
public class OrderDesk
readonly Dictionary<string, decimal> prices = new() { ["mug"] = 8.00m, ["tea"] = 4.50m };
int nextId = 1;
public async Task<Receipt> PlaceAsync(string customer, IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> lines, CancellationToken ct = default)
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(customer)) throw new ArgumentException("A customer is required.", nameof(customer));
if (lines.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("An order needs at least one line.");
await Task.Yield();
decimal total = 0m;
foreach (var line in lines)
if (!prices.TryGetValue(line.Sku, out var price)) throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Unknown product {line.Sku}.");
total += price * line.Quantity;
return new Receipt(nextId++, customer.Trim(), lines, total);
Write `public class OrderDeskTests` with at least **five** `async Task` tests:
- a happy path that checks the whole receipt with **one** `Assert.Equivalent`;
- the second order gets the next id;
- each refusal (blank customer, no lines, unknown product) with an awaited `Assert.ThrowsAsync<...>`.
Six planted bugs.
starter: Receipt receipt = await desk.PlaceAsync("Ada", [new OrderLine("mug", 2)], TestContext.Current.CancellationToken);
solution: Receipt receipt = await desk.PlaceAsync("  Ada ", lines, Ct);
Receipt second = await desk.PlaceAsync("Grace", [new OrderLine("tea", 1)], Ct);
var ex = await Assert.ThrowsAsync<ArgumentException>(() => desk.PlaceAsync(customer, [new OrderLine("mug", 1)], Ct));
var ex = await Assert.ThrowsAsync<KeyNotFoundException>(() => desk.PlaceAsync("Ada", [new OrderLine("cup", 1)], Ct));

target: public record OrderLine(string Sku, int Quantity);
public record Receipt(int Id, string Customer, IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines, decimal Total);
public async Task<Receipt> PlaceAsync(string customer, IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> lines, CancellationToken ct = default)
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(customer)) throw new ArgumentException("A customer is required.", nameof(customer));
if (lines.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("An order needs at least one line.");
if (!prices.TryGetValue(line.Sku, out var price)) throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Unknown product {line.Sku}.");
return new Receipt(nextId++, customer.Trim(), lines, total);

mutants.name: an order without lines is accepted
replace: if (lines.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("An order needs at least one line.");

hints: Build the expected receipt with `new Receipt(1, "Ada", lines, 20.50m)` and compare with `Assert.Equivalent(expected, receipt)`.
Pass a customer with spaces around it in the happy path: the trimming is behaviour too.
For the refusals: `await Assert.ThrowsAsync<ArgumentException>(() => desk.PlaceAsync("   ", [new OrderLine("mug", 1)], Ct));`, and the same for no lines and an unknown SKU.
steps.explain: `Assert.Equivalent` compares the receipt's public data, list included, and names the field that differs, so one assertion covers trimming, quantity and total. Awaiting each `ThrowsAsync` is what makes the refusal tests real.
